1.pericope_label: The exordium of the Song: heaven and earth summoned, and the doctrine like rain

schools.summary: Gill reports the reading that makes the second verse a prayer and prefers to take it as a prophecy of what would be, sets the doctrine here against the law as cooling against fiery and gentle rain against storm, and holds with Keil that the verb of the third verse is to proclaim the name rather than to call upon it. Calvin explains the magnificent opening as a guard against the people's pride, since the world will endure no strain that does not tickle the ear with praise while this one stigmatises their perverse nature and incorrigible contumacy and was meant to echo daily from their own tongues; he rejects those who resolve the future tense into the optative, holding that the speaker celebrates the fruitfulness the Spirit imparts rather than asking for it, and notes that the clause about publishing the name stands last though it gives the reason for what precedes.

Henry takes the appeal to heaven and earth as a solemn appeal to the truth of what follows and the justice of God's proceedings, and argues that these would sooner hear than a perverse people, since they have never revolted from obedience to their Creator and will rise up in judgment; he also observes that this is the first place in Scripture where God is called a Rock, a figure for power and faithfulness that cannot be moved and for the shelter those countries found in their rocks against sun and tempest.

Clarke derives the word for doctrine from a root meaning to gain over the heart by persuasive speech, notes that the Greek version renders it by a term for a weighty sententious saying, and reads the figure of the rain progressively, beginning slowly and increasing until the whole canon of revelation is complete. Wesley makes the lifeless creatures both an accusation of a people duller of hearing than they and a body of witnesses, and finds the point of the rain in the softening of hearts.

Keil sets the scale of the song, which covers the whole future history of Israel and carries the marks of prophetic testimony, and quotes a description of it as soaring to the loftiest heights, concise and pictorial, rough and penetrating yet full of the holiest solemnity, a witness against a disobedient nation and a miniature of its author's whole life; he finds the point of comparison in the refreshing and fertilising power of dew and rain, and holds that the verb means to proclaim the name rather than to call upon it. Ellicott notes that the opening is almost identical with a prophet's except that the two words for hearing change places, and renders 'doctrine' rather as learning, that which is received, building on it a chain in which everything from the Father of lights is handed from one heavenly messenger to another until it reaches a man in the form he can best receive.

debates: Whether the second verse is a wish or a promise: Gill reports the reading that makes it a prayer and prefers a prophecy, and Calvin names those who resolve the future tense into the optative and rejects them, holding that the fruitfulness is celebrated rather than requested
What the verb of the third verse means: Gill and Keil both reject 'call upon the name' in favour of 'proclaim the name'
outliers: Keil quotes a description of the song as rough, penetrating and sharp yet full of the holiest solemnity, and as a miniature of the whole life of the man who spoke it
Clarke reads the rain falling drop by drop and increasing as a figure of revelation completed by degrees down to the closing of the canon
Ellicott makes the word for doctrine mean what is received, and traces a chain of transmission from the Father of lights through heavenly messengers to the heart of man
Henry observes that this is the first place in Scripture where God is called a Rock

4.pericope_label: The Rock whose work is perfect, and the foolish people who requite him

schools.summary: Gill notes that the word for the Rock stands first for emphasis and is written with an enlarged letter to mark the greatness of the person meant, identifies it with the rock struck in the wilderness. Calvin warns against taking the attributes generally and without reference to this passage, since the perfection of God's works stands deliberately against the rebellion of the people and any defect in them would have furnished an excuse; he says the recital of benefits begins in order to expose the ingratitude to greater infamy, and doubts not that the hearers would have raged had they not known the speaker was already called to die.

Clarke reports that eminent critics and a great Jewish authority render the word as Creator, origin or first cause, so that the line would run that he is the first principle and his work is perfect, while allowing that the usual rendering gives a very good sense since rocks were the ordinary places of defence; on the following verse he sets out two conjectural renderings, one following the Samaritan text, and denounces as a bad doctrine without foundation in the text the common interpretation that God's children have their spots but that sin in them is not as sin in others. Wesley takes the Rock for stability of nature and invincible power and for fixedness in counsel and promise, so that any sad change proceeds from the man and not from God; he treats the stain as proof that these are not God's children at all and adds that the text does not affirm that God's children have any spot whatever; and he presses the three verbs of the reproach, bought as redeemed from bondage, made as formed into a peculiar people, established as favour renewed and not withdrawn.

Ellicott makes the name of the Rock a characteristic of the whole song, traces it to the smiting of the rock at Horeb and observes that the confession was carried in the very names of Israel's leaders; he says no such combination of all the words for uprightness, sincerity, equity and reliability occurs elsewhere in Scripture, reports that many interpreters give the next two lines up as hopeless because of the number of possible interpretations and offers his own after consulting a learned Hebrew, and notes that the reproach opens with an exclamatory question, that question and exclamation bear one name among the rabbinical writers, and that the verb rendered 'bought' is the word used at the birth of Cain. Keil explains the difficult clause as parenthetical apposition, takes the word in the moral sense of a stain, observes that no difficulty would have arisen had it stood after the subject, and treats the reproach as the expansion of the theme, the perversity showing itself in repaying with apostasy the God to whom the nation owed its existence.

debates: What the title at the head of the song means: Clarke reports eminent critics, an ancient version and a great Jewish authority for Creator or first cause and would render the line accordingly, while Gill, Ellicott and Wesley all build on the rendering 'Rock', which Clarke himself allows gives a very good sense

How to construe the clause about the spot: Ellicott reports that many give it up as hopeless and offers a rendering reached with help, Clarke gives two conjectural versions and attacks the common devotional reading as a bad doctrine unfounded in the text, Wesley denies that the text affirms any spot in God's children at all, and Keil resolves it as a parenthetical apposition
outliers: Gill observes that the first word of the song is written with an enlarged letter to mark the greatness of the person meant

Ellicott points out that the confession of God as a Rock was carried in the personal names of Israel's leaders, one meaning that God is a rock, another that the Almighty is a rock, a third that the bearer was redeemed by the rock
Clarke denounces as unfounded the doctrine that God does not see the sins of his children as he sees the sins of his enemies
Ellicott notes that the verb rendered 'bought' is the word used by Eve at the birth of Cain

7.pericope_label: Remember the days of old: the nations divided and Israel taken as the Lord’s portion

schools.summary: Gill reads the summons prospectively, listing deliverances still future when the words were spoken, from the judges and the days of David down through the captivity to the age of the Maccabees, since he takes the whole song as addressed to a much later generation; on the division of the earth he names the generation in whose days it was divided and whose name records it, and presses that men did not seize what they pleased but each had his parcel allotted by the Lord himself, and he extends the title of the Lord's portion to a spiritual Israel chosen and taken into covenant. Calvin makes the verse an explanation of the one before, given so that a people inflated by their present standing should consider not what they are but from what they were taken, since men who forget that all they have proceeded from God are blinded by their dignity; and he insists that nothing moved God but his own good pleasure, the words assigning not any superiority in the people but a dignity depending wholly on gratuitous election.

Henry reads the summons as an appeal to the records, bidding them keep in remembrance the history of those days and the providences concerning the old world and the patriarchs, in which a constant series of mercies may be traced and the working of things towards what had now come to pass.

Clarke reports on another's authority that these verses give express warrant for believing the earth was divided very early by divine command and probably by lot, assigns a continent to each of Noah's sons with Palestine held in reserve as the Lord's portion, and calls the whole movement the general migration commanded to Noah and passed on to his sons; on the next verse he alone turns the saying round and finds the astonishment in the exchange, since as holy souls take God for their portion so God takes them for his, representing himself as happy in his followers, while a man seeking an earthly portion has little commerce with the Most High. Wesley holds that the lands were disposed so as to reserve room for the numbers Israel would become, and that the hearts of several peoples were so guided that the posterity of Canaan, already accursed, settled in the very country intended for Israel so that when their iniquities were ripe they might be rooted out; he reduces the choice to one sentence, that it is no wonder God had so great a regard to a people chosen out of all mankind for his peculiar portion.

Keil takes the summons as a call to reflect on what the Lord had done and identifies the years of generation after generation with the deliverance out of Egypt, reaching back before Moses and a little past him; he takes the boundaries to be fixed with reference to the number of the sons of Israel, so that from the forming of nations God had cared for this people, says the choice was made before the nation existed, and explains the figure of the last clause as a measuring cord, then a piece of land measured off, and so applied to the people. Ellicott notes only that the first verse falls plainly into four parts.

debates: What 'the days of old' covers: Keil identifies them with the deliverance out of Egypt and the times just before and after Moses, Henry with the history of the old world and the patriarchs, while Gill reads the song as addressed to a much later generation and lists deliverances still future when it was spoken, down to the age of the Maccabees

How the division of the nations bears on Israel: Clarke reports a scheme assigning a continent to each of Noah's sons with Palestine reserved, Wesley holds that the Canaanites were deliberately settled there so that they might be rooted out when ripe, and Keil and Gill keep to the reserving of room and the allotting of each people's parcel
outliers: Clarke calls the early dispersion the general migration and holds it to have been commanded to Noah and passed on by him to his sons
Gill names the generation in whose days the earth was divided and whose very name records the division
Clarke finds the astonishment of the verse in the exchange, that as holy souls take God for their portion, so God takes them for his
Keil explains the word for 'lot' as a measuring cord, then a piece of land measured off, and so applied figuratively to the nation

10.pericope_label: Found in the wilderness, borne on eagles’ wings, and fed with the fat of the land

schools.summary: Gill reports a rabbinic account of the eagle as merciful to her young, not entering the nest suddenly but first making a noise and shaking it so that they may be fitter to receive her reads the high places as towers and fortified cities and cites a paraphrase to that effect. Calvin observes that had the intention been to record every instance of God's kindness the recital must have begun from Abraham; he says the exclusive clause is spoken by anticipation to take away every pretext from a people whose standing plea when they imported foreign gods was that God was not thereby robbed of his honour; and he dismisses as frivolous the notion that the land was called high for being the navel of the earth, weighing the usage by which men go down into Egypt and up into Judea and inclining to take the term of its excellency.

Clarke on the eagle offers two accounts and takes the harsher, that she disturbs the nest to oblige the young to leave it, as God by his plagues obliged a reluctant people to leave a place marked for destruction; he states that help came from no other quarter and that the Egyptian gods could not save their own worshippers; and he claims that all the verbs describing the land stand in the future, so that the passage is prophecy of a prosperity still to come in which even the rocky country would be made fertile. Wesley denies that chance is meant by the finding, distinguishes the manifestation in Egypt from the eminent finding in the wilderness, presses that the young are carried as on the wings and not in the claws and reports the belief that the eagle does usually so carry them, draws the inference that the hearers were the more unworthy for giving idols a share in worship owed to God alone, says that to ride upon is in Scripture to subdue, explains the honey by bees in the rock holes and the oil by olives bearing best in rocky ground.

Ellicott points out that the first verse stands in the pictorial present in Hebrew and that finding is a word common to both Testaments for God's first revealing of himself to a man, and notes that the metaphor of the kidney fat is carried over literally from the Hebrew and that this was the fat the law reserved for the altar. Keil keeps the eagle figure whole, a bird teaching its young to fly and shielding them with watchful affection, and takes the driving over the high places as a figure for the victorious subjugation of a land.

debates: What the eagle is doing: Clarke offers both that she excites the young to fly and that she disturbs the nest to force them out, and takes the second, applying it to the plagues driving out a reluctant people, whereas the rabbinic account Gill reports makes the disturbance a mercy that prepares the young to receive her

Whether the description of the land is past or future: Clarke insists that all its verbs stand in the future and reads the passage as prophecy of a prosperity still to come, while Keil, Gill and Wesley take it of the conquest and possession already in view
outliers: Wesley reports the belief that the eagle usually carries her young upon her wings rather than in her claws
Ellicott notes that the fat of the kidneys, used here as a figure for the finest wheat, was the fat strictly reserved for God's altar by the Levitical law
Calvin rejects the notion that Judea was called high as being the navel of the earth, and weighs instead the idiom of going down into Egypt and up into Judea
Gill cites a paraphrase that reads the high places as the towers of the land of Israel

15.pericope_label: Jeshurun waxed fat and kicked, and forsook the Rock

schools.summary: Gill derives the name from a word for upright and observes that the people ought to have been such and professed to be; he dissents from the whole reading of the next verse, taking the word rendered strange gods to mean simply others, pointing out that the people were not guilty of idolatry after the return from Babylon, and referring it to the other saviours and messiahs set up after the rejection of Christ, none having been attempted before his coming; he reports a version making the Rock the rock of thy kindred, a near kinsman and a brother by incarnation. Calvin quotes the proverb that satiety breeds violence but lays the blame on men's own depravity, cautions that jealousy is ascribed to God only figuratively since he is free from all passions while insisting that the grossness of the sin requires such terms, and fixes the aggravation of the closing reproach, that they did not fall through ignorance but wilfully stifled a knowledge of God which ought to have shone in every heart.
Henry sorts the apostasy into two counts, the first being security and sensuality, pride and insolence and the other common abuses of plenty and prosperity.

Clarke derives the name from a root for uprightness and reads it as showing that a people once really walking in righteousness would in the time foretold not merely revolt but fight against God, like a full-fed horse that will not bear the harness but breaks away and kicks at his master; he surveys the word rendered devils across the versions, the Syriac, Chaldee, Targums and Samaritan keeping the original term while the Latin, Greek, Arabic, Persic, Coptic and Anglo-Saxon give devils or demons, the Arabic using the plural of the name of Satan; and he keeps to his earlier rendering of the title as the first cause and fountain of being. Wesley takes the name as reminding the people what they professed and shaming them for degenerating from it, glosses the jealousy as the rage of a man whose ground is their falseness to a God accepted as husband, explains that the idols were brought into the world by devils who manifested themselves in them while the Gentiles were deluded with the pretence that they were lower gods, and refers the Rock either to God or to the Christ whom the Israelites tempted.

Ellicott takes the name as a diminutive and a term of endearment, either the child of the upright or the beloved Israel, since the letters of the diminutive of Israel slightly abbreviated would yield it, and notes that it belongs to this book and one prophet only, that two Targums render it simply Israel while a third keeps the word, and that the Greek translates it the beloved one; he observes that an apostle repeats the phrase about sacrificing to devils, renders the clause about new gods literally as those that came from close at hand and compares the idol made out of firewood, and on the closing reproach offers as another possible rendering that the Rock has begotten thee forgetful, noting that the word he so renders is usually taken as a verb although no such verb is found elsewhere and has been invented for this passage. Keil says only that these verses expand the one before them.

debates: What the name Jeshurun means: Gill, Clarke and Wesley all derive it from a word for upright and draw a reproach from the derivation, while Ellicott makes it a diminutive of endearment, the beloved little Israel, supported by the Targums and the Greek

Whether the strange gods are literal idols: Calvin, Wesley, Clarke and Keil all take the verses of idolatry, while Gill renders the word simply as others and refers it to false messiahs set up after the rejection of Christ, since the people were no longer idolaters after the return from Babylon
outliers: Clarke likens the apostasy to a full-fed horse that will not bear the harness but breaks away and kicks at his master
Calvin cautions that jealousy is ascribed to God only figuratively, since he is free from all passions, while insisting that the grossness of the sin requires the language
Ellicott observes that the word he would render 'forgetful' is usually taken as a verb although no such verb occurs anywhere else, so that it has been invented for this passage
Wesley explains that the Gentiles professed to worship God in their idols and were deluded with the pretence that these were a sort of lower gods

19.pericope_label: The Lord rejects his sons, hides his face, and kindles the fire of his anger

schools.summary: Gill refers the seeing to a later rejection keeps the first clause of the retaliation on home ground by referring the no-god to the false Christs that arose after the true one and applies the fire to the burning of the city and temple. Calvin makes the seeing a statement about forbearance in judgment, that God does not act hastily or become alienated without weighing the case, as elsewhere he goes down to see whether a city's cry is what it is reported to be, while adding that God can need no such examination; he describes the retaliation as God becoming the open enemy after withdrawing for a time and repaying in kind, exalting barbarous nations against those who had set empty phantoms in antagonism with him, and he keeps the fire as metaphor while insisting that more is expressed here than in the many other places where the figure occurs.

Henry sets the passage in its place, since the song follows the order of the predictions in the chapter before, so that the resolves of divine justice come immediately after the revolt; and he warns that we deceive ourselves if we think God will be mocked by a faithless people who play fast and loose with him, having delighted in them and now rejecting them with detestation.

Clarke renders the first line more literally, that the Lord saw and through indignation reprobated his sons and daughters, corrects the clause about faith to mean that there is no steadfastness in them and they can never be depended on, being fickle because faithless, calls the retaliation a very pointed promise of the calling of the Gentiles applied by an apostle to that event, and takes the fire for the deepest destruction and total extermination, reading the foundations of the mountains as the strongest fortresses and finding the whole fulfilled in the last Roman destruction of the city. Wesley marks that they were sons and daughters by calling and profession, says they are perfidious and have broken a covenant solemnly made defines the no-people as nations without the knowledge and fear of God which he calls the foundation of all true policy and government, and extends the fire past this world, the misery it brings here being only a faint resemblance of a misery without end.

Keil takes the seeing as no more than the causal link between apostasy and punishment and renders the description as a generation full of perversities. Ellicott makes the point about faith exactly, that the word is not used in the sense of belief or confidence but as when we speak of keeping or breaking faith, so that these are children with whom no faith will be kept; he reports that an apostle uses the retaliation to prove that Israel had been informed of the calling of the Gentiles beforehand and pairs it with a prophet's words about being found of them that sought him not, and on the fire he notes that a prophet quotes the line and reports a rabbinic gloss making the foundations of the mountains the city founded upon them.

debates: What 'the Lord saw' implies: Calvin makes it forbearance in judgment and a due weighing of the case, while noting that God needs no examination, Keil takes it as no more than the causal link between the apostasy and the punishment, and Clarke as the moment of being justly incensed

How far the fire reaches: Clarke and Gill find it fulfilled in the Roman destruction of Jerusalem and its fortifications, Calvin keeps it as an intensified metaphor, and Wesley extends it past this world, the misery here being a faint resemblance of a misery without end
outliers: Ellicott insists that 'faith' here does not mean belief or confidence but the keeping of faith, so that these are children with whom no faith will be kept
Wesley defines the no-people as nations lacking the knowledge and fear of God, which he calls the foundation of all true policy and government
Ellicott reports a rabbinic gloss making 'the foundations of the mountains' the city that is founded upon them
Clarke observes that of the fortifications of the city not one stone was left

24.pericope_label: The arrows spent, and the judgment stayed for the sake of God’s name

schools.summary: Gill supplies the local colour of the famine, a paraphrase rendering the first stroke as being swollen with famine, a word a historian used of the siege of the city, and a rabbinic reading that would make it the hairs of hunger; he localises the two swords as the besieging army outside and the weapons of the factions within, presses the opening verb of the turn as meaning that God could have said or might have said, since it was in his power and justice to do it, and alone identifies the enemy otherwise, as the adversary of mankind and of God himself who stirs up wrath and blasphemy in the hearts of men. Calvin reduces the scourges to the standing triad of pestilence, famine and the sword and explains that specimens are adduced because generalities would not have affected the hearers; on the turn he describes God as representing himself under the character of a man, meditating opposite determinations and restraining his vehemence, so that the final judgment was suspended for no other reason than regard to his own glory, which would otherwise have been exposed to the taunts of the nations.

Henry marks the turn as surprising intimations of mercy after so many terrible threatenings, mercy wholly undeserved, which rejoices against judgment and shows that God has no pleasure in the death of sinners, and states the ground, that in jealousy for his own honour God will not make a full end.

Clarke numbers the scourges as arrows shot in succession, famine, burning heat taken either of a rainless sky or of boils and pestilential fevers, the plague, the multiplying of wild beasts and the poisonous serpents; on the fear of wrath he reports that some would refer the word not to the enemy but to God and gives their rendering, that indignation for the adversary deters him lest the enemies be alienated and claim the strength of their own hands had done this, his own point being that unless the punishment proved whose hand it was the heathen would have drawn the wrong conclusion. Wesley describes the famine as burning and parching the inward parts and blackening the face, takes the heat of fevers or carbuncles, and keeps the common reading of the fear as the enemy's rage and furious reproaches against God's name, adding that the fear of it is ascribed to God after the manner of men.

Keil divides the field of the slaughter exactly, the sword sweeping away the men outside while the defenceless perish in the chambers from alarm, and names a scholar who applied the second word to hunger and plague and says he is wrong, since it means a sudden mortal terror; he holds that the people had deserved to be utterly destroyed and were spared for another reason than their own. Ellicott offers alternatives for the verb about the adversaries, either that they should misunderstand the matter or that they should take note of it as a strange thing.

debates: Whose anger is feared: Clarke reports a rendering that refers the word to God's own indignation for the adversary rather than to the enemy's wrath, while Wesley, Keil and Gill keep the common reading of the enemy's rage and misconstruction
Who the enemy is: Gill alone identifies him as the adversary of mankind and of God himself, where the others take the heathen nations who would claim the victory as their own
outliers: Gill reports a paraphrase rendering the famine as a swelling, and notes that a historian used the same word of the siege of the city
Gill also reports a rabbinic reading that would make the phrase 'the hairs of hunger', since a famishing man's hair grows
Keil names a scholar who applied the word for terror to hunger and plague and rejects the application, the word meaning a sudden mortal terror
Calvin describes God as representing himself under the character of a man, meditating opposite determinations and restraining his own vehemence at the obstacles he meets

28.pericope_label: A nation void of counsel, the rout, and the vine of Sodom

schools.summary: Gill holds that the prophecy against the one people has been discharged and that their enemies are now in view, and carries that through the passage, applying the vine at the end to corrupt professors within the empire that destroyed the city; he guards the wish that follows against being made the words of God, since it would then furnish an instance of an unsuccessful wish in him and an argument that a man may make himself wise if he will, whereas they are the words of Moses under a spirit of prophecy. Calvin reads the opening the other way, assigning the cause why the memory of the people had almost been blotted out, that their folly was incurable and not one drop of sagacity existed in them; he says the token of the rout is chosen as peculiarly striking, since a people who once routed mighty armies are now conquered by a few; and he denies that the vine refers, as some make it, to the punishment the people deserved, taking it for an invective against their corrupted morals.

Clarke takes the phrase about the latter end of their latter times and makes it the days of the Messiah who was to spring from them, takes the enemies as witnesses who concede the point since they often acknowledged the irresistible power of the God who fought for Israel and adds a parallel from a Latin poet, and reads the vine of Israel, taking the grapes for their actions and the clusters for their united as well as their several deeds. Wesley calls the enemies a foolish people who therefore judge falsely of things, makes the latter end what their end will be and that judgment will overtake them at last though God spare them long, fills out the two verbs of the rout as sold for bondslaves and shut up as in a net, and says that dear-bought experience forced the enemies to own that this God was stronger than they and their gods together.

Ellicott renders the opening phrase literally as perishing in counsels, or perhaps as spoiling the plans of the Lord, and sets beside it the resolution of men who devised devices against a prophet in the confidence that counsel would never fail from the wise; he renders the next clause as discernment about their hereafter and what they will miss if they fail to fulfil it, notes that the verb rendered 'sold' is here used of the Lord for the first time and becomes common later, proposes on a rabbinic authority that the clause about judges means that our enemies are lords over us and that the verse stands as a parenthesis, and states expressly that the vine is Israel's and not the enemies'. Keil states the rout conditionally, that a wise Israel could easily have conquered all its foes in the power of its God and was given up only because it had forsaken its rock.

debates: Whom the passage describes: Gill holds that the prophecy against Israel is discharged and that the enemies are now in view, carrying that through to the vine at the end, and Wesley agrees at the opening, whereas Ellicott states expressly that the vine is Israel's and not the enemies', and Clarke and Calvin read the whole of Israel

What 'our enemies themselves being judges' means: Clarke and Wesley take the enemies as witnesses forced to concede the point, while Ellicott proposes on a rabbinic authority that they are lords over us and reads the verse as a parenthesis
outliers: Gill guards the wish of the passage against being taken for the words of God, which would furnish an instance of an unsuccessful wish in him and an argument that a man may make himself wise if he will
Clarke reads 'their latter end' as their latter times, meaning the days of the Messiah who was to spring from them
Ellicott notes that the verb rendered 'sold' is here applied to the Lord for the first time and becomes common in the later history
Calvin denies that the vine of Sodom refers, as some make it, to the punishment the people deserved, taking it for an invective against their morals

34.pericope_label: Vengeance laid up in store, and the Lord judging his people

schools.summary: Gill takes what is laid up in store of principles and practices kept in the divine memory to be produced at the proper time; on the vengeance he draws a fence, that it belongs to a divine person only and not to any heathen deity of that name, nor to Satan and his angels, nor to any of the sons of men in a private capacity, and notes that the ancient versions and the Targums render the clause as a promise to repay; and on the last verse he denies that the Lord is upbraiding Israel and, on the authority of the Targums, puts the taunt in the mouth of the enemy, adding that the words may be rendered impersonally and in the singular. Calvin reports and rejects the view that the store is of punishments rather than crimes, since the ungodly treat God's forbearance as connivance; on the judging of the people he states both the threatening and the consoling sense and resolves them by a distinction, that an apostle may accommodate to another purpose what was set down for the consolation of the godly; and on the last verse he sets out the two options and argues against the enemy's taunt from the plural form of the word for gods.

Clarke supplies the legal figure behind the sealing, that deeds binding men to fulfil conditions at a stated time were sealed and laid up in places of safety, so that justice stands pledged while the time and manner remain sealed; he reports a commentator who refers the verse about vengeance not to Israel at all but to the Canaanites, holds both that God has right to punish them as their Sovereign and that he will change his manner of conduct when their power is wholly gone and not one strong place is left untaken, and makes the closing question God's own expostulation, suggesting that it may look forward to the preaching of the Gospel in the latter days. Wesley takes the store to be their sins, remembered punctually and sealed up as in a bag though the long-suffering may make them think them forgotten; he presses that those who think they stand unmoveable shall fall, that the due time is not so soon as some expect but when the measure of their sins is full, and that Scripture often calls near what is many hundred years off; and he reads the judging of the people as pleading their cause and delivering them, the discourse turning into a more comfortable strain.

Ellicott doubts the usual reference of the pronoun to what follows and suggests it may point back to the vine that yielded wild grapes; he points out that the sentence about vengeance is quoted in two epistles, once together with the opening of the next verse, corrects the following clause to read of the time when their foot shall slide, holds on the strength of the apostolic use that to judge here means to punish and not to defend, and offers a rendering by which God will be comforted over his servants. Keil takes the turn as the moment when the people are convinced of the worthlessness of idols.

debates: What is laid up in store: Calvin reports the view that it is the punishments and prefers the crimes, Wesley and Gill agree that the sins are meant, and Ellicott doubts the usual reference and suggests the failure of the vine

Whether 'the Lord shall judge his people' threatens or consoles: Ellicott follows the apostolic use and says it means to punish and not to defend, Wesley reads it as pleading their cause and delivering them, and Calvin states both and allows that an apostle may accommodate to another purpose what was written for consolation

Who asks where their gods are: Gill puts the taunt in the enemy's mouth on the authority of the Targums, Calvin argues against that from the plural form and prefers a pious exultation of the faithful, and Clarke makes it God expostulating to awaken them
outliers: Clarke explains the sealing from the practice of sealing up deeds and laying them in places of safety until the appointed time
Gill denies that vengeance belongs to any heathen deity of that name, or to Satan and his angels, or to private men
Clarke reports a commentator who refers the verse about vengeance to the Canaanites rather than to Israel
Wesley observes that Scripture calls near what is many hundred years distant, because distance in our measures of time is nothing in God's

39.pericope_label: See now that I am he: the oath, the whetted sword, and the arrows drunk with blood

schools.summary: Gill directs the opening words both to a people in their low estate and to the enemies who insult them, notes that the lifted hand is the gesture used in swearing and is ascribed to a divine person while reporting that the same action is sometimes used merely to excite attention, takes the conditional clause as the suppressed half of an oath whose consequence is left to be concluded by the hearer, describes the sword drawn and polished and whetted so that when brandished it glitters like lightning. Calvin notes that those who gave the preceding verses to the unbelievers must now bring God in abruptly, whereas he takes the words as a confirmation of the holy boasting just put into the mouths of the faithful; he reports a rendering that would join the lifted hand to the verse before and prefers to begin a new sentence, resolves the conditional particle into an adverb of time so that the destruction of the enemies is certain as soon as God takes up arms while adding that God wants no weapons, and describes the massacre intended as leaving no end to the vengeance until the earth is full of blood and corpses.
Henry treats the passage as the conclusion of the song and hears in it a demand for the glory of self-existence, the name by which the speaker had first been made to know God.

Clarke states that God alone can save and God alone destroy while the idols can neither hurt nor help, and adds that the mercy is as great as the justice since he is as ready to save the penitent as he was to punish the rebellious; on the last verse he holds that the word rendered 'revenges' never bears that sense, which has made the place perplexed and obscure, and sets out another scholar's version ending with the hairy head of the enemy. Wesley reduces the opening to a lesson learned by sad experience, what vain and impotent things idols are, makes the oath two clauses, reads the conditional plainly as a condition of beginning and glosses the second noun as the instruments of judgment, a metaphor from warriors taking their weapons in hand, distinguishes the captives as sorely wounded though not utterly killed, and takes the last clause to mean that once the vengeance begins it will make a full end.

Ellicott observes that many passages in one prophet run very close to the opening sentence without exactly reproducing it, and that the following clause was taken up afterwards in a woman's song of thanksgiving; on the last verse he keeps the received sense and renders literally from the blood of the slain and of the captivity, from the beginning of revenges upon the enemy, adding that judgment must begin at the house of God as it did in a prophet's vision where it began at the sanctuary. Keil marks the lifted hand as the close of the ode and calls the promise it ends with one full of comfort for all the servants of the Lord.

debates: What the conditional clause about whetting the sword does: Gill takes it as the suppressed half of an oath whose consequence is left unstated, Calvin resolves the particle into an adverb of time so that nothing is left in suspense, and Wesley reads it plainly as a condition of beginning

How the closing verse is to be rendered: Clarke holds that the word translated 'revenges' never bears that sense and reports a version ending with the hairy head of the enemy, while Ellicott keeps the received sense and renders from the beginning of revenges upon the enemy
outliers: Clarke sets the mercy beside the justice, God being as ready to save the penitent as he was to punish the rebellious
Ellicott notes that the clause about killing and making alive was taken up afterwards in a woman's song of thanksgiving
Gill reports that the lifting of the hand is sometimes used merely to excite the attention of hearers, though here it means an oath
Ellicott observes that judgment must begin at the house of God, as in the vision where it began at the sanctuary

44.pericope_label: The song delivered, and the charge to set the heart upon it

schools.summary: Gill supposes that Moses came from the tabernacle, on the authority of a Targum which calls it the house of instruction, and says of the closing charge that it was no light or trifling matter but one of great consequence, obedience being attended with rewards and disobedience with punishment. Calvin draws a lesson from the mere fact of the repetition, that it shows how far Moses was from all ambition, since at the very close of his life he did not fear to irritate every mind against him and make the memory of his own name hateful, while his authority is confirmed from the other side by the silence and submissiveness of hearers who let themselves be dealt with so severely.

Henry supposes that Moses spoke the song to as many as could hear him while Joshua at the same time delivered it in another assembly to as many as his own voice would reach, and draws the point that, coming from the mouth of both governors, the one laying down the office and the other taking it up, the people could see that the two were of one mind.

Clarke supposes that Moses came from the tabernacle because the ode had been given him there, takes the closing charge as another proof that all the denunciations of divine wrath, delivered though they are in an absolute form, were only declaratory of what God would do if the people rebelled, and says of the promise attached that instead of being cut off they would be preserved and made prosperous in the land. Wesley gives the same reconstruction of the two assemblies as Henry and adds that Joshua as well as Moses would thus be a witness against them if ever they forsook God.

Keil states that the two spoke the song together and that the closing exhortation impressed the importance of the commandments once more, and observes that this account comes from the hand that supplied the appendix to the books of Moses. Ellicott alone stops at the name, asking why Joshua should be called Hoshea here when the name had apparently been changed when he went with the eleven others to search out the land, and answering that now, when the man is about to lead the people to the conquest, the reader is reminded of the change and of what it meant, that the salvation of the Lord was to be shown forth through him; he corrects the charge to read that they may command their children, observes that for a long time to come the knowledge of the law must have depended largely on personal instruction, cites a rabbinic parallel for setting the heart on all the words, renders the last verse as meaning that the thing is not too light for them, and marks it as the last time in the book that the people are told the very end of their existence in the land was the keeping of this law.

debates: Whether the threats of the song are absolute: Clarke takes the closing charge as proof that all the denunciations, delivered though they are in an absolute form, were only declaratory of what God would do if the people rebelled
outliers: Keil observes that this closing account comes from the hand that supplied the appendix to the books of Moses

Ellicott asks why Joshua is called by his older name here, and answers that the change is recalled at the moment he is about to lead the conquest, since the salvation of the Lord was to be shown forth through him
Calvin finds in the repetition of the song a proof of how far its author was from ambition, since he did not fear at the close of his life to make the memory of his own name hateful
Ellicott notes that for a long time to come the knowledge of the law must have depended very largely on personal instruction

48.pericope_label: Moses is called up to Nebo to see the land and to die

schools.summary: Gill fixes the day as that on which the reading of the law and the song was finished, gives the month and day, reports a Targum which makes it the day of his death and another calendar that places it later in the same month, adds that the peak named is a summit of the range, takes the command plainly as meaning that after the view of the land he was to expect death and submit to it willingly, and names two faults in the reason given for the sentence, an unbelief that doubted whether God would give water to so rebellious a people and a giving way to passion and wrathful words. Calvin denies that these verses stand in their proper order, since Moses was warned of his death before the song was composed and the place had been pointed out before Joshua was substituted for him, adding that an inverted order of narration is not unusual; and he weighs what the sentence cost, since death in itself would not have been so bitter but the cause wounded the holy man grievously, in that he saw himself shut out by God's just vengeance from the common inheritance on account of his own guilt, which to the pious is more afflictive than many deaths.

Henry asks why, having finished his work, Moses should wish to live a day longer, and turns to the reminder of the old sin for which he was kept out of the land, drawing the lesson that it is good for the best of men to die repenting the infirmities they are conscious of, while adding that those who have a believing prospect may die with comfort whenever God calls, notwithstanding the sins they remember against themselves.

Clarke gives the meaning of the mountain range as the mount of the passages, that is, of the people when they entered the promised land, and answers those who have supposed that Moses was translated rather than that he died, since if so his brother was translated too, what is said of the death of the one being said of the death of the other. Wesley asks why, his work being finished, he should wish to live longer, observes that though he had formerly prayed to go over Jordan he is now entirely satisfied and says no more of it, adds that the peak named is a ridge of the range, and marks the timing of the reminder, that God recalls a sin committed long before, repeating that it is good for the holiest of men to die repenting even of their early faults.

Ellicott says the day meant is that on which the song was spoken in the ears of all Israel, and supplies the history of the command to go up, that it had been given once before and was answered then by the prayer for a successor which was granted, so that everything narrated between that passage and this may be counted preliminary to the departure; he points out that the particular peak on which the death was to happen had not been named until now. Keil states the charge itself, to go up, to see the land given for a possession, and to die there and be gathered to his people as his brother had been on another mountain.

debates: Whether the narrative stands in order: Calvin argues that it does not, since Moses was warned of his approaching death before the song was composed and the place of it had been pointed out before Joshua was appointed, while Gill, Ellicott and Wesley take the day at face value as the day the song was delivered

Whether Moses died or was translated: Clarke reports the supposition that he was translated and answers that it would prove his brother translated too, since what is said of the death of the one is said of the death of the other
outliers: Gill reports a Targum making the day of the song's delivery the very day of Moses' death, and another calendar that places it later in the same month
Clarke explains the name of the mountain range as the mount of the passages, of the people entering the promised land
Ellicott notes that the particular peak on which Moses was to die had not been named in the earlier form of the command
Calvin holds that exclusion from the common inheritance on account of his own guilt is more afflictive to a pious man than many deaths
